MSK–SKIN · MODULE II · LECTURE COMPANION

Bone & Cartilage
Histopathology

From extracellular matrix and microscopic architecture to osteoclast signaling, bone remodeling, cartilage mechanics, and characteristic disease patterns.

Source: Bone & Cartilage lecture, Oct. 27, 20256 learning objectivesImages retained from lecture
START HERE

Learning objectives

  1. Define bone characteristics, functions, classifications and component parts.
  2. Describe mineral and organic bone matrix and their mechanical contributions.
  3. Identify bone-forming, sensing, lining, and resorbing cells, including their appearance and activities.
  4. Explain modeling, remodeling, mineralization, bone turnover, and resorption.
  5. Compare hyaline, elastic, and fibrocartilage by structure, composition, growth, location, and function.
  6. Recognize the histopathology of osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, osteomalacia, osteogenesis imperfecta, and Paget disease.

Big picture

Bone is a living, vascularized composite: type I collagen resists tension, hydroxyapatite resists compression, and coordinated cellular activity continually reshapes the matrix. Cartilage is an avascular, hydrated matrix optimized for compression and low-friction movement; its poor intrinsic repair capacity makes articular injury clinically consequential. Understanding the normal matrix tells you why the diseases look different on imaging and histology.

Matrix composition → tissue mechanics → cell activity → remodeling or failed repair → pathology

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 01

Architecture: classifying and identifying bone

What bone does

Bone provides biomechanical levers for muscular movement, protects internal organs, contains hematopoietic marrow, and stores calcium (approximately 99% of the body's calcium according to the accompanying lecture handout).

ClassificationTypical examplesRecognition / role
LongFemur, tibia, humerus, metacarpalsLong axis and shaft; movement and load transfer
ShortCarpals, tarsalsCompact shapes; stability and limited movement
FlatScapula, cranial bonesBroad protection and muscle attachment
IrregularVertebrae, sacrum, mandibleComplex shapes and specialized functions
SesamoidPatellaEmbedded within tendon; protects tendon and improves leverage

Parts of a long bone

The diaphysis is the shaft, the metaphysis lies between shaft and end, and the epiphysis forms the end. The physis or epiphyseal growth plate separates developing regions until growth ends; the physeal scar is the mature remnant. Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces.

Compact versus cancellous

FeatureCortical / compactCancellous / trabecular
Adult skeletal mass~80%~20%
Surface-to-volume ratio (lecture)2.520
Typical locationDiaphysis; outer shellMetaphysis, epiphysis; internal bone
Core contributionStrength, movement, protectionMultidirectional support and mineral homeostasis
Structural unitOsteonTrabecula

From gross anatomy to the microscope

The osteon is composed of concentric lamellae around a longitudinal Haversian canal carrying vessels and nerves. Volkmann canals connect longitudinal vascular canals transversely. Osteocytes occupy lacunae and extend processes along canaliculi. The outer periosteum has fibrous and inner osteogenic layers; Sharpey fibers anchor it into bone. The endosteum lines the internal marrow and trabecular surfaces. Flat cranial bones include a spongy diploë between compact outer and inner tables.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why do osteocytes rely on canaliculi while marrow is well vascularized?

Osteocytes are embedded within hard mineralized matrix; their cellular processes and surrounding canalicular fluid permit nutrient diffusion and signaling toward nearby blood vessels.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 02

Bone matrix: why the material behaves as it does

The lecture describes bone by wet weight: approximately 60% hydroxyapatite mineral, 30% organic matrix, and 10% water. About 90% of the organic component is type I collagen, with the remaining organic material including ground substance (GAGs) and noncollagenous proteins, prominently osteocalcin.

MUST KNOW
Mineral gives stiffness/compressive strength; collagen provides tensile toughness. If either component fails, bone becomes mechanically abnormal—but by different mechanisms.

Why mineralization is a separate process

Osteoblasts first deposit osteoid (unmineralized organic matrix). Mineral then nucleates and accumulates in this scaffold, using calcium and phosphate. Alkaline phosphatase on matrix vesicles helps supply local phosphate. Systemic regulators highlighted in the lecture include vitamin D, PTH, calcitonin and FGF23 (phosphate regulation).

Osteoblast deposits osteoid → matrix vesicle / ALP activity → calcium-phosphate crystal deposition → mineralized bone
COMMON CONFUSION
Osteoid is not the same as finished mineralized bone. Accumulated osteoid indicates that matrix production has occurred, but successful mineralization has not.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A biopsy contains abundant unmineralized osteoid. Which part of bone formation is impaired?

Mineralization of osteoid, rather than necessarily the initial synthesis of the collagen-rich organic scaffold.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 03

Bone cells: build, crunch, sense, and line

Bone's key cellular lineages are not interchangeable: osteoclasts descend from hematopoietic/monocyte lineage precursors, whereas osteoblasts, osteocytes and bone-lining cells are mesenchymal lineage cells.

CellAppearance / markerJob and lineage
OsteoclastLarge, multinucleated; ruffled border; lysosomes; TRAP+Hematopoietic origin. Resorbs organic matrix using cathepsin K and mineral using acid; occupies Howship lacunae.
OsteoblastSurface-lining, cuboidal; ALP+Mesenchymal origin. Synthesizes and deposits osteoid on a bone surface.
OsteocyteIn mineralized lacunae; processes in canaliculi; high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratioFormer osteoblast. Nonmitotic mechanosensor that coordinates formation and resorption.
Bone lining cellFlat, elongated, spindle-shaped nucleusInactive osteoblast-derived surface barrier and reactivatable osteoblast population.

Osteoclast differentiation: the RANK axis

M-CSF supports the osteoclast lineage, and RANKL from osteoblasts/osteocytes binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to stimulate differentiation and activity. OPG is a decoy receptor for RANKL, thereby reducing osteoclast stimulation.

EXAM TRAP
RANKL is pro-resorption; OPG is anti-resorption. They are opposing regulators, not both activators.

Osteocytes as the network coordinator

Osteocytes communicate through processes in canaliculi and gap junctions. They release RANKL and M-CSF to promote osteoclasts, OPG to restrain osteoclast activity, and sclerostin / Dkk1 to inhibit osteoblast-driven formation.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A signal that neutralizes RANKL should change which cell behavior?

It should reduce osteoclast maturation/activity and therefore decrease bone resorption.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 04

Deposition, turnover and structural adaptation

Modeling versus remodeling

Modeling involves independent osteoclast or osteoblast action at different surfaces; it changes bone size and shape, especially during growth. Remodeling is coupled sequential resorption and formation in a basic multicellular unit (BMU): osteoclasts remove old bone and osteoblasts refill the cavity with osteoid that mineralizes. “Coupled” does not necessarily mean balanced.

Where the BMU works

On trabecular bone, remodeling occurs along a trabecular surface, often under a bone-lining-cell canopy. In cortical bone, osteoclasts form a cutting cone and osteoblasts follow to refill the tunnel concentrically; the Haversian canal remains centrally. The handout additionally identifies matrix-stored TGF-β1 and IGF-1 as factors released by resorption that help recruit osteoblast progenitors.

When formation and resorption are out of balance

ContextMechanistic directionNet effect
MenopauseEstrogen loss → resorption exceeds formationBone loss
AgingLess effective osteoblast formation relative to resorptionBone loss
BisphosphonatesInhibit osteoclast-mediated resorptionPreserve/increase bone mass
Intermittent PTH analogsStimulate osteoblast-associated formationAnabolic bone gain

Additional agents named in the handout: abaloparatide (PTHrP analog) and romosozumab (sclerostin-targeted antibody) as osteogenic therapies.

Reading out turnover in a patient

Iliac crest histomorphometry is a specialized method for evaluating metabolic bone disorders. Circulating markers are more widely used in assessment contexts: resorption correlates with type I collagen telopeptides/crosslinks and TRAP; formation with type I procollagen propeptides, osteocalcin, and alkaline phosphatase.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · If remodeling is coupled, can bone mass still fall? Why?

Yes. Sequential resorption and formation are coupled, but if each BMU removes more matrix than is replaced, repeated cycles cause net bone loss.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 05

Cartilage matrix, growth and histologic identification

Cartilage is avascular and aneural, with chondrocytes nourished by diffusion through a highly hydrated extracellular matrix. The lecture emphasizes poor healing capacity following damage. Its principal matrix components include type II collagen fibrils and proteoglycan aggregates such as aggrecan associated with hyaluronic acid.

How cartilage withstands pressure

Negatively charged GAGs repel one another and attract water. That hydrated gel distributes compressive loading, while collagen helps restrain swelling and withstand tensile strain. The territorial matrix around lacunae is relatively GAG-rich and stains more basophilically; the lighter region between lacunae is interterritorial matrix.

Chondroblasts, chondrocytes and growth

Chondroblasts in the inner perichondrium synthesize type II collagen and proteoglycan matrix. Once surrounded by matrix, they are termed chondrocytes and occupy lacunae. Appositional growth adds cartilage from perichondrial precursors at the surface. Interstitial growth occurs when existing chondrocytes divide and elaborate matrix internally; recent daughter cells appear in isogenic groups. Unlike bone, cartilage can grow interstitially.

Three cartilage types

TypeECM / light microscopyExamplesMechanical role
HyalineType II fibrils and proteoglycans; smooth “glassy” matrix, fibers not visible by light microscopyTrachea, costal cartilage, growth plate, articular surfacesSupport, low-friction joint movement, compression resistance
ElasticHyaline-like matrix plus visible elastic fibers; more cellularExternal ear, epiglottisFlexible structure that tolerates bending
FibrocartilageType II plus abundant visible type I collagen bundles; rows of chondrocytesIntervertebral disc, pubic symphysis, meniscusTensile and compressive strength

Perichondrium normally covers cartilage, with important exceptions: articular cartilage and growth plates lack it; the handout also states that fibrocartilage lacks perichondrium because it transitions into dense connective tissue.

COMMON CONFUSION
Hyaline and elastic cartilage both contain type II collagen; elastic also has elastic fibers. Fibrocartilage also contains type I collagen bundles, which are visible by light microscopy.

Why cartilage injury is different

Because articular cartilage lacks blood vessels, spontaneous repair is limited. The lecture describes microfracture surgery: perforations into subchondral bone allow marrow-derived cells to enter a defect and produce repair tissue, typically fibrocartilage. Fibrocartilage does not reproduce the normal loading behavior of the original hyaline articular surface. The cited lecture study reports a 66% long-term failure rate and mean failure time of 4.0 years for the studied cohort, not a universal individual outcome.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A histology slide shows chondrocytes in rows between thick eosinophilic collagen bundles. Which cartilage?

Fibrocartilage: the visible type I collagen bundles and linear chondrocyte arrangement are the distinguishing features.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 06

Histopathology: recognize the failed process

The lecture lists five clinically important disorders. The underlying discriminator is what fails: matrix composition, mineralization, resorption/formation balance, remodeling organization, or articular cartilage integrity.

DisorderCore defect / mechanismPathology recognition
Osteogenesis imperfectaType I collagen abnormality (organic matrix)Brittle, fracture-prone bone; impaired tensile integrity
Osteomalacia / ricketsImpaired mineralization of osteoidIncreased unmineralized osteoid; rickets affects developing growth plates
OsteoporosisLoss of bone mass from remodeling imbalanceReduced trabecular connectivity/thickness with otherwise ordinarily mineralized remaining bone
Paget disease of boneHigh turnover with disorganized remodelingAbnormal, disorganized architecture; classic mosaic/cement-line pattern is a board association
OsteoarthritisDegeneration and damage of articular cartilageCartilage fibrillation and loss; poor intrinsic healing

Three distinct paths to fragility

Osteogenesis imperfecta: deficient collagen quality → low tensile toughness
Osteomalacia: deficient mineral deposition → soft, poorly stiffened bone
Osteoporosis: diminished bone quantity → weakened skeletal structure
FIRST AID CONNECTION
Osteogenesis imperfecta is classically linked to COL1A1/COL1A2 abnormalities, recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss and dentinogenesis imperfecta. These are board-recognition extensions beyond the primary histology comparison.
FIRST AID CONNECTION
Osteomalacia / rickets can reflect vitamin D deficiency and may present with bone pain, muscle weakness and growth abnormalities in children. Distinguish impaired mineralization from simple reduced bone mass.
FIRST AID CONNECTION
Paget disease may show elevated alkaline phosphatase with calcium and phosphate often normal, and a mosaic lamellar pattern. Its key distinguishing mechanism is accelerated but disorganized remodeling.

Osteoclast activity: too much versus too little

The lecture contrasts excessive resorption contributing to osteoporosis with deficient osteoclast function producing osteopetrosis. Osteopetrosis is a dense-bone disorder, not an indication that the bone is automatically normal or robust.

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
Osteopetrosis: defective osteoclast resorption can cause abnormally dense but brittle bone and impaired marrow space, with possible anemia or cranial-nerve compression. This provides a useful contrast to low-density osteoporosis.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient has reduced bone mass with normally mineralized remaining matrix; another has broad seams of unmineralized osteoid. Which condition is which?

Reduced mass with maintained mineralization is osteoporosis; excess unmineralized osteoid is osteomalacia.

FINAL SYNTHESIS

Master these before moving on

  1. Differentiate mineral from collagen: hydroxyapatite resists compression; collagen resists tension. This predicts how matrix diseases cause fragility.
  2. Know the lineages and markers: osteoclast = hematopoietic/TRAP/multinucleate; osteoblast = mesenchymal/ALP/cuboidal.
  3. Separate formation, resorption, and regulation: osteocytes sense loading and use RANKL, OPG and sclerostin to direct turnover.
  4. Separate modeling from remodeling: independent surface action versus coupled sequential BMU activity; coupling does not guarantee balance.
  5. Identify cartilage with collagen and arrangement: hyaline = glassy type II; elastic = elastic fibers; fibrocartilage = thick type I bundles plus chondrocyte rows.

The most useful First Aid connections

  1. Type I collagen defects → osteogenesis imperfecta → fractures plus extra-skeletal collagen clues.
  2. Defective mineralization → osteomalacia/rickets → excess osteoid and vitamin D/mineral regulation.
  3. Bone resorption/formation mismatch → osteoporosis → trabecular thinning and fractures.
  4. High, disorganized remodeling → Paget disease → mosaic-like lamellar architecture and increased ALP.
  5. RANKL–OPG signaling → osteoclast differentiation → mechanistic basis for antiresorptive therapies.
